910.name: Prehistoric Finland & Sámi Heritage
910.description: Finland's long prehistory from post-glacial settlement through the Comb Ceramic and Corded Ware cultures, the arrival of Finno-Ugric peoples, and the indigenous Sámi presence stretching back millennia.

sub_clusters.name: Post-Glacial Settlement & Stone Age
sub_clusters.description: The earliest colonisation of Finland after the last Ice Age, the Suomusjärvi culture, Comb Ceramic culture, and the gradual differentiation of Finno-Ugric language groups.

sub_clusters.name: Sámi Indigenous Heritage
sub_clusters.description: The Sámi as the indigenous people of northern Fennoscandia, their semi-nomadic reindeer-herding culture, shamanic traditions (noaidi), and their relationship with incoming Finnic populations.
key_events: Earliest Sámi presence documented in northern Fennoscandia through archaeological evidence (c. 1500 BCE onward)

920.name: Swedish Crusades & Medieval Finland
920.description: The Swedish Northern Crusades that brought Finland into the Swedish realm and the Catholic Church, the founding of Turku (Åbo) as the administrative centre, and Finland's incorporation into Scandinavian politics.

sub_clusters.name: Swedish Crusades to Finland
sub_clusters.description: The three Swedish Crusades to Finland (traditionally dated 1155, 1249, 1293), the Christianisation of the Finns, the founding of Turku Cathedral, and the establishment of Viborg (Viipuri) fortress on the Russian frontier.
key_events: Second Swedish Crusade under Birger Jarl incorporates Finland proper into the Swedish realm (1249)

sub_clusters.name: Medieval Finnish Society
sub_clusters.description: The Treaty of Nöteborg (1323) establishing the Finnish-Russian border, Finnish representation in Swedish politics, the Kalmar Union period, and the development of a distinct Finnish identity within the Swedish realm.

sub_clusters.name: Finnish Folk Culture & Oral Tradition
sub_clusters.description: The Kalevala-metre oral poetry tradition, rune singing in Karelia and Finland proper, pre-Christian belief systems persisting alongside Christianity, and the cultural roots of Finnish national identity.

930.name: Finnish Reformation & Swedish Great Power Era
930.description: The Reformation in Finland and the creation of written Finnish by Mikael Agricola, Finland's role as Sweden's eastern bulwark during the Great Power era, and the devastating effects of continual warfare with Russia.

sub_clusters.name: Mikael Agricola & the Finnish Reformation
sub_clusters.description: Mikael Agricola, the 'father of written Finnish,' translated the New Testament into Finnish (1548) and created the Finnish literary language, while the Lutheran Reformation reshaped Finnish society.
key_events: Mikael Agricola publishes the first Finnish-language book, the ABC-kiria (1543)

sub_clusters.name: Swedish Great Power & the Eastern Frontier
sub_clusters.description: Finland as Sweden's eastern frontier: the Club War peasant uprising (1596–1597), Finnish Hakkapeliitta cavalry in the Thirty Years' War, the founding of Helsinki (1550), and the University of Turku (1640).

930.name: Great Wrath & Russian Pressure
930.description: The catastrophic Russian occupations — the Great Wrath (1714–1721) and Lesser Wrath (1742–1743) — that devastated Finland, the collapse of Swedish Great Power, and the growing strategic vulnerability of Finland.

sub_clusters.name: Great Northern War & the Great Wrath
sub_clusters.description: Russia's occupation of Finland during the Great Northern War (1714–1721), known as the 'Great Wrath' (Isoviha) for its devastating impact — famine, forced labour, and deportations killing a third of Finland's population.

sub_clusters.name: Gustavian Era & Russo-Swedish War
sub_clusters.description: Gustav III's war with Russia (1788–1790), the Anjala conspiracy of Finnish officers, and the final Russo-Swedish War (1808–1809) that ended Swedish rule over Finland.

940.name: Grand Duchy of Finland under Russia
940.description: Finland's autonomous status as a Grand Duchy within the Russian Empire, the flourishing of Finnish national identity through the Kalevala and the Finnish language movement, and the Russification crises that galvanised the independence movement.

sub_clusters.name: Autonomous Grand Duchy & National Awakening
sub_clusters.description: The Diet of Porvoo (1809) where Tsar Alexander I guaranteed Finnish autonomy, Helsinki as the new capital (1812), Elias Lönnrot's compilation of the Kalevala (1835), and the early Finnish language movement.
key_events: Elias Lönnrot publishes the Kalevala, the Finnish national epic (1835)

sub_clusters.name: Language Strife & National Culture
sub_clusters.description: The Fennoman vs. Svecoman struggle over Finnish and Swedish as the national language, the Language Decree of 1863, Sibelius's Finlandia (1899), and the golden age of Finnish national romanticism in art and architecture.

sub_clusters.name: Russification & Resistance
sub_clusters.description: Governor-General Bobrikov's Russification campaigns (February Manifesto 1899), Bobrikov's assassination (1904), the 1905 general strike, Finland granting universal suffrage including women (1906 — first in Europe), and the path to independence.

950.name: Finnish Independence & Civil War
950.description: Finland's declaration of independence (6 December 1917), the brutal Civil War between Whites and Reds (January–May 1918), and the young republic's consolidation during the interwar years.

sub_clusters.name: Independence & Civil War (1917–1918)
sub_clusters.description: The Russian Revolution's enabling of Finnish independence, the declaration of 6 December 1917, the devastating Finnish Civil War (27 January – 15 May 1918), White victory with German assistance, and the deep national trauma.
key_events: Finnish Civil War between Whites and Reds leaves approximately 37,000 dead (1918)

sub_clusters.name: Interwar Republic & Reconciliation
sub_clusters.description: The adoption of a republican constitution (1919), the Åland Islands question settled by the League of Nations, the Lapua movement's far-right challenge, and the gradual national reconciliation between Whites and Reds.

950.name: Winter War & Continuation War
950.description: Finland's heroic resistance against the Soviet invasion in the Winter War (1939–1940), the alliance of convenience with Germany in the Continuation War (1941–1944), and the preservation of Finnish independence at a heavy territorial cost.

sub_clusters.name: Winter War (1939–1940)
sub_clusters.description: The Soviet invasion of 30 November 1939, Finnish resistance on the Mannerheim Line, the stunning victories at Suomussalmi and Raate Road, international admiration for Finnish 'sisu,' and the Moscow Peace Treaty ceding Karelia.
key_events: Finland repels Soviet forces at the Battle of Suomussalmi during the Winter War (1939–1940)

sub_clusters.name: Continuation War & Lapland War
sub_clusters.description: Finland's co-belligerency with Germany (1941–1944), the Soviet Vyborg–Petrozavodsk offensive (1944), the Moscow Armistice, and the Lapland War expelling German forces from northern Finland.

sub_clusters.name: Paris Peace Treaty & War Reparations
sub_clusters.description: The 1947 Paris Peace Treaty's territorial and financial terms, the massive Soviet war reparations ($300 million) that paradoxically drove Finnish industrialisation, and the war-responsibility trials.

960.name: Finlandization & Cold War Neutrality
960.description: Finland's delicate balancing act during the Cold War — maintaining democratic capitalism while deferring to Soviet foreign policy concerns — known as 'Finlandization,' under the long presidency of Urho Kekkonen.

sub_clusters.name: Paasikivi–Kekkonen Doctrine
sub_clusters.description: The FCMA Treaty with the Soviet Union (1948), Urho Kekkonen's 25-year presidency (1956–1981), the policy of active neutrality, hosting the CSCE Helsinki Accords (1975), and the costs and benefits of Finlandization.

sub_clusters.name: Nordic Welfare Model & Industrialisation
sub_clusters.description: Finland's rapid industrialisation and urbanisation, the building of a comprehensive Nordic welfare state, war reparations driving industrial capacity, and the emergence of high-technology sectors.

960.name: Contemporary Finland
960.description: Post-Cold War Finland: EU membership (1995), Nokia's rise and fall, the world-renowned education system, and the historic decision to join NATO (2023) ending decades of military non-alignment.

sub_clusters.name: EU Membership & Nokia Era
sub_clusters.description: The post-Soviet economic crisis, EU accession (1995), eurozone membership (1999), Nokia's transformation of Finland into a tech powerhouse, and Finland's consistently top-ranking performance in education (PISA).

sub_clusters.name: Startup Ecosystem & Gaming Industry
sub_clusters.description: The post-Nokia pivot to startups (Slush conference), the mobile gaming boom (Supercell, Rovio), the world's happiest country rankings, and Finland's tech-driven innovation economy.

sub_clusters.name: NATO Accession & Security Pivot
sub_clusters.description: Russia's invasion of Ukraine catalysing Finland's historic NATO application (2022) and accession as the 31st member (4 April 2023), ending 75 years of military non-alignment and transforming European security architecture.
key_events: Finland joins NATO as the 31st member state (4 April 2023)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
